Publishing proactively is fine for your own work-product — artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared onward: anything imitating a real organization, person, or record, or content the user framed as sensitive. Build those as files, and let the user decide whether they get a URL.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

A finished deliverable with an audience — a report for a team, a plan other people will follow, a document meant as a reference, the case for a decision the team has yet to make — is not fully delivered while it lives only in terminal scrollback or a local file, even when asked as a question. Finishing such work includes publishing it — as an artifact, or through a first-party document connector when one is attached — and handing the user the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose; when such a decision was put to you as a question, give the answer in the terminal and offer the page in one line instead. **Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this user, a published page can do more than static HTML — read the user's live or connected data, remember what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — the page saves new versions of itself), keep state shared across viewers, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question of its own, store files people add, or hand the viewer a file to save — declared via the `capabilities` input. **Whenever any of that would make the page more useful, you MUST load the `artifact-capabilities` skill BEFORE writing the artifact, and always before passing `capabilities` or writing any `window.claude.*` runtime code** — it tells you what's available to this user and how to use it. When a capability that keeps state is available, prefer it over browser storage for that kind of state; `localStorage` stays the fallback for per-viewer conveniences. Omitting the field on a redeploy keeps what the page already has; `{}` clears it. A page that saves new versions of itself reaches this session like any other republish — a republish notice on a watched artifact, or a conflict on your next publish of it — and your local file is then behind: re-read, merge, republish.

**Before writing the file — a skill-instructed `.md` included — you MUST load the `artifact-design` skill** to calibrate how much design investment this particular request warrants. Format is not part of that decision — the Format rule above settles it, and Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass. icon.description: Optional. One short generic word for the artifact's tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map — a plain signifier, not a product or brand name. Omit when republishing to keep the current icon.

limit.description: list only: maximum artifacts to return (default 25).

title.description: Title for the artifact — the name shown in the browser tab and gallery. description.description: One-sentence subtitle shown on the gallery card. Say what the page is or does.

label.description: A short name for this publish, max 60 chars (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional — a few words, not a description.

text.description: reply only: the reply text. Plain text, at most 4096 bytes of UTF-8.

cursor.description: comments only: continue a listing that ended with a "more threads not listed" line — pass the cursor value that line names to render the threads it could not fit.

acknowledge_duplicate.description: reply only: post even though a Claude reply already stands after every "sent to Claude" request on the thread. out_dir.description: read_db: when given, each returned document is written as pretty-printed JSON to <out_dir>/<collection path>/<doc_id>.json (directories created as needed) and the result lists the files instead of the document contents — use it for large documents or many of them.

capabilities.description: Runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. The control plane is the authority on valid names and config shapes. An empty object clears any previously stored declaration; omit the field on a redeploy to carry the stored declaration forward unchanged. Before declaring any capability, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill for the current contract and per-capability guidance.

contract.description: The artifact's runtime version. Omit to keep its current version (the default); 'latest' to upgrade; a specific version to pin or roll back. Changing it changes how the published page behaves — pass only when the author explicitly intends the change, never as a side effect of editing.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:

content.text:
Here's the lay of the land: body text currently renders in **Open Sans**, loaded as a webfont via Astro's font API (`astro.config.mjs`) and wired in as the `--font-sans` token (`src/styles/global.css:6`), which Tailwind's preflight applies to `<body>` by default. Headings stay on Literata (serif) and your name uses the handwriting font — those wouldn't be touched either way.

Your proposed stack is just the classic Apple/system-UI fallback chain (San Francisco on Apple devices → Helvetica Neue/Helvetica/Arial elsewhere). There isn't one unambiguous way to "add" it — where it goes in the stack changes the actual visible result:

**Plan A — Replace Open Sans entirely (recommended if you want the native/system look)**
- Set `--font-sans` to the system stack, drop the Open Sans entry from `astro.config.mjs` and its `<Font>` preload tag.
- Result: every visitor sees their OS's native UI font (San Francisco on Mac/iOS, Segoe UI-ish via fallback on Windows since it'd drop to Arial, Roboto-adjacent on Android via Arial). Zero webfont latency/FOUT, lighter page weight, feels like a native app. You lose the distinct "Open Sans" character as your brand voice for body copy.

**Plan B — System font first, Open Sans as fallback**
- `--font-sans: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Helvetica Neue", Helvetica, Arial, var(--font-open-sans), sans-serif;`
- Result: Mac/iOS Safari and Chrome-on-Mac users (where `-apple-system`/`BlinkMacSystemFont` resolve) never see Open Sans — the system keyword wins over the loaded webfont. Everyone else (Windows, Linux, Android) still gets Open Sans. Inconsistent look across platforms, and you'd still be paying to load/preload Open Sans for users who'll never see it.

**Plan C — Open Sans first, system stack as the fallback/safety net (standard practice)**
- `--font-sans: var(--font-open-sans), -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Helvetica Neue", Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif;`
- Result: no visible change for anyone once Open Sans loads — it's just a better fallback than the generic `sans-serif` you'd otherwise end on (covers the instant before the webfont loads, and any failure case). Doesn't address your actual question of "is the system font nicer," since Open Sans still wins everywhere.

**Plan D — Leave it as is.**

Given you're asking "is this nicer," that's a look-and-feel call only you can make — A and B produce visibly different results depending on platform, so I don't want to guess which you're after.

content.text:
A quick honest note first: I don't have a stored profile on you from a "knowledge base" — nothing persists across sessions yet in this project's memory. What I actually know comes from this codebase and conversation: software engineer + social entrepreneur, into AI ethics/data sovereignty/a "post-extractive web", you work at Liva Healthcare, co-founded a few startups before, hobbies are photos/guitar/bouldering (currently commented out of the index), you've got a story-driven Copenhagen album, and a "digital garden" with seedling/budding/evergreen essays. That's the material I'm working from.

**On the looping trip-video idea:** I'd push back gently before building it. Two real snags:

1. Browsers block autoplay audio — a video "with simple music playing over and over" can't actually autoplay with sound unless it's muted, or the visitor clicks play first. So the idea as literally stated isn't buildable as a passive loop; it'd need to be muted-by-default (visual only) or opt-in.
2. It's in tension with the site you've already built. Everything here — the CLS-safe image pipeline, the story-driven albums instead of autoplay carousels, the "post-extractive web" line in your own description — reads as a deliberate stance against attention-grabbing, autoplaying media. A looping video-with-music on the homepage is the classic extractive-web pattern (autoplay, loop, hijack attention). It'd undercut the thing you're actually saying about yourself.

A muted, silent loop (no music) is a tamer version that avoids both problems — but even then it's a media-weight/motion-respecting tradeoff worth being deliberate about.

**Other directions that fit what's already here, roughly cheapest → most involved:**

- **A "now" strip** — a few plain lines near the top: current trip/location, what you're building, what you're reading or listening to. Pure text, zero media cost, extends the garden metaphor you already have (seedling/budding/evergreen) into "what's alive right now."
- **Lean into your own color names** — you literally named your accent tokens `evening` and `sunset`. Tie the accent (or a thin gradient) to the visitor's actual local time of day instead of (or alongside) the light/dark toggle. Very "yours," zero new assets, no autoplay anything.
- **One still photo, not a video** — pull a single real shot from your own albums (you already have the ImageKit pipeline for this) as a quiet hero image behind the intro text. Static, fast, no motion/audio questions at all.
- **An opt-in audio clip** — a short guitar recording behind a play button near your handwriting signature. Intimate and unique, but the visitor chooses to hit play — no autoplay conflict.
- **Muted looping clip, your original idea, tamed** — one of your trip clips, silent, small, behind/above the intro text, with a tap-to-unmute control and respecting `prefers-reduced-motion` (pause for those who've asked for it).

Checked the raw HTML/CSS (it's a Framer site, but the technique itself is framework-agnostic). Here's exactly how it works:

**Structure:** behind the actual nav content there's a separate fixed container, same width as the viewport, ~108px tall (matching the header height), `z-index` *below* the nav links, `pointer-events: none` (so it's purely visual, doesn't block clicks). Inside it are **8 stacked, absolutely-positioned divs**, each `inset: 0` (same size, fully overlapping).

Each of the 8 divs has two things:
1. `backdrop-filter: blur(Npx)` where N doubles every layer: `0.078125px → 0.15625 → 0.3125 → 0.625 → 1.25 → 2.5 → 5 → 10px`.
2. `mask-image: linear-gradient(to bottom, transparent, black, black, transparent)` — but each layer's gradient stops are shifted down 12.5% from the last (layer 1 occupies the 0–37.5% band, layer 2 the 12.5–50% band, and so on, 8 layers × 12.5% = the full height).

The mask controls *where that layer's blur is visible*. Stacked together, this produces a smooth ramp — almost no blur at the very top, increasing continuously to a full 10px blur by the bottom of the bar — instead of the hard, flat edge you get from one `backdrop-filter: blur(10px)` over the whole header (which looks like a pane of glass was dropped in with a visible seam). This exact pattern is the standard "progressive/variable blur" trick for nav bars (same idea Apple uses natively in iOS/macOS toolbars).

**Why it's cheap:** zero JavaScript — no scroll listener recalculating anything. `backdrop-filter` is GPU-composited, and the masks are static gradients computed once. The browser just composites 8 pre-blurred, pre-masked layers; nothing reruns per frame on scroll.

Worth noting: your own git history already has `0f4f97f Adding top bar fade` followed later by `4e208b8 Removing fade` — so you tried a (presumably simpler, single-layer) version of this before and pulled it. This progressive-mask version is more work but avoids the hard-edge look that a flat fade/blur gets you, which may be exactly what felt off last time.

Want me to implement this behind your header (`src/layouts/Layout.astro`), reusing your existing `--color-mist`/`--color-charcoal` as the base so it still adapts to light/dark?

That pasted markup answers it — two things I had wrong:

1. **The gradient direction is `to top`, not `to bottom`.** I'd flipped which blur value went on which layer while keeping the gradient pointing down; the real site instead keeps blur values on their original layers and just flips the gradient axis. Those aren't equivalent.
2. **That's exactly why your "height looks smaller" question has a real answer:** with `to top`, layer 8 (the strongest, `10px` blur)'s mask only resolves inside the box between `87.5%` and `100%` — its `black 100%, black 112.5%` plateau is mostly *past* the top edge, clipped off. So the strongest blur never gets to hold a flat plateau at all — it only ever reaches full strength right at the very top pixel. The *visible*, strongly-blurred band ends up compressed into roughly the top 12% of the container, not spread across the whole thing. My version spread the strong blur across the top 37.5% instead — which is exactly why mine looked taller/heavier than the reference, even at the same container height.

Fixing both — reverting to the original blur-to-layer mapping and flipping the direction to `to top`:
